/-!
# Steiner Systems

A Steiner system $S(t, k, n)$ is a collection of $k$-element subsets (called blocks) of
an $n$-element set such that every $t$-element subset is contained in exactly one block.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steiner_system)
- [Large Steiner Systems](https://epoch.ai/frontiermath/open-problems/large-steiner-systems)
  by Kunal Marwaha
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace SteinerSystems

/--
An $S(t, k, n)$-Steiner system is a collection of $k$-element subsets (called blocks) of
$\{0, \ldots, n-1\}$ such that every $t$-element subset is contained in exactly one block.

This is the standard notation from combinatorics, where:
- $n$ is the number of points
- $k$ is the block size
- $t$ is the covering parameter (every $t$-subset is in exactly one block)
-/
structure SteinerSystem (t k n : ℕ) where
  /-- The blocks of the Steiner system. -/
  blocks : Finset (Finset (Fin n))
  /-- Every block has exactly $k$ elements. -/
  block_card : ∀ B ∈ blocks, B.card = k
  /-- Every $t$-element subset is contained in exactly one block.
  Note: We use `.filter.card = 1` instead of `∃!` because `∃! B ∈ blocks, R ⊆ B` desugars to
  a quantifier over all `Finset (Fin n)`, which loses `Decidable` and breaks `native_decide`. -/
  cover_unique : ∀ R : Finset (Fin n), R.card = t → (blocks.filter (R ⊆ ·)).card = 1

/-- Notation for Steiner systems: `S(t, k, n)` denotes a Steiner system with
covering parameter `t`, block size `k`, and `n` points. -/
scoped notation "S(" t ", " k ", " n ")" => SteinerSystem t k n

/--
A constructive witness for a large Steiner system: concrete values of $n$, $k$, $t$
satisfying $n > k > t > 5$, $t < 10$, $n < 200$, together with an explicit Steiner system.
-/
structure LargeSteinerSystemWitness where
  /-- The size of the ground set. -/
  n : ℕ
  /-- The block size. -/
  k : ℕ
  /-- The covering parameter. -/
  t : ℕ
  h_nk : n > k
  h_kt : k > t
  h_t_lower : t > 5
  h_t_upper : t < 10
  h_n_upper : n < 200
  /-- The explicit Steiner system. -/
  system : S(t, k, n)

/--
Construct an $S(t, k, n)$-Steiner system with $n > k > t > 5$, $t < 10$, and $n < 200$.

No example of a Steiner system with $t > 5$ is known, despite a 2014 existence theorem
by Keevash showing that such systems must exist for sufficiently large $n$.

*Reference:* [Large Steiner Systems](https://epoch.ai/frontiermath/open-problems/large-steiner-systems)
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem large_steiner_systems : Nonempty LargeSteinerSystemWitness := by
  sorry

/--
Sanity check: the Fano plane is an $S(2, 3, 7)$-Steiner system.

The Fano plane consists of $7$ blocks of size $3$ over $7$ points,
where every pair of points is contained in exactly one block.
-/
@[category test, AMS 5]
def fano_plane : S(2, 3, 7) :=
  ⟨{{(0 : Fin 7), 1, 3}, {1, 2, 4}, {2, 3, 5},
    {3, 4, 6}, {0, 4, 5}, {1, 5, 6}, {0, 2, 6}},
   by native_decide, by native_decide⟩

It was constructed by Witt (1938) and is closely related to the Mathieu group $M_{12}$.

-/

/--
**Existence of $S(5, 8, 24)$**: The large Witt design.

There exists a unique Steiner system $S(5, 8, 24)$, known as the large Witt design.
It was constructed by Witt (1938) and is closely related to the Mathieu group $M_{24}$.
This is one of only two known Steiner systems with $t = 5$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem steiner_system_5_8_24 : Nonempty S(5, 8, 24) := by
  sorry

/--
**There are infinitely many Steiner systems with $t = 4$.**

Keevash (2014) proved that for any fixed $t$ and $k$, a Steiner system $S(t, k, n)$
exists for all sufficiently large $n$ satisfying the necessary divisibility conditions.
Since there are infinitely many such admissible $n$, this implies infinitely many
$S(4, k, n)$ systems exist (for any fixed $k > 4$). The proof is nonconstructive.

Explicit examples include $S(4, 5, 11)$ (the unique system, related to the Mathieu
group $M_{11}$) and $S(4, 7, 23)$ (related to the Mathieu group $M_{23}$).

Only nontrivial systems with $4 < k < n$ are counted: for every $n$ the single block
$\{1, \dots, n\}$ is an $S(4, n, n)$, and all $4$-subsets of an $n$-set form an $S(4, 4, n)$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem infinitely_many_steiner_t4 :
    {s : Σ k n : ℕ, S(4, k, n) | 4 < s.1 ∧ s.1 < s.2.1}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
**There are infinitely many Steiner systems with $t = 5$.**

Keevash (2014) proved that for any fixed $t$ and $k$, a Steiner system $S(t, k, n)$
exists for all sufficiently large $n$ satisfying the necessary divisibility conditions.
This settles the long-standing open problem of whether infinitely many $S(5, k, n)$
systems exist. The proof is nonconstructive.

Only two explicit examples are known: $S(5, 6, 12)$ and $S(5, 8, 24)$, both Witt
designs related to the Mathieu groups $M_{12}$ and $M_{24}$ respectively.

Only nontrivial systems with $5 < k < n$ are counted, for the same reason as in
`infinitely_many_steiner_t4`.
No Steiner system with $t \geq 6$ has been explicitly constructed, though Keevash's
result guarantees their existence nonconstructively as well.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem infinitely_many_steiner_t5 :
    {s : Σ k n : ℕ, S(5, k, n) | 5 < s.1 ∧ s.1 < s.2.1}.Infinite := by
  sorry

findings.description: The docstring says, “This is one of only two known Steiner systems with t = 5.” The two Witt designs do not exhaust the known explicit Steiner 5-designs. This is a factual error in the background documentation; the Lean existence statement and its explicit witness are correct.
findings.source_evidence: Brouwer’s “Steiner systems,” linked from the cited Wikipedia article, explicitly lists S(5,6,v) for v = 12, 24, 36, 48, 72, 84, 108, 132, 168, 244, and also S(5,7,28): https://www.win.tue.nl/~aeb/graphs/S.html. Marwaha’s table, linked from the Epoch problem’s accompanying PDF, likewise states that S(5,6,24), S(5,6,36), and S(5,6,48) are known: https://marwahaha.github.io/steinersystems/.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace “one of only two known Steiner systems with t = 5” with “one of the two classical Witt designs with t = 5,” without claiming these exhaust the known examples.

findings.description: The docstring repeats the incorrect assertion that there are only two known Steiner systems with t = 5. Additional explicit Steiner 5-designs are known. The Lean statement Nonempty S(5,8,24) is faithful and does not assert this erroneous classification.
findings.source_evidence: Brouwer’s reference lists numerous other Steiner 5-designs, including S(5,6,24) and S(5,7,28): https://www.win.tue.nl/~aeb/graphs/S.html, section “Steiner 5-designs.” The problem author’s linked table independently lists S(5,6,24), S(5,6,36), and S(5,6,48): https://marwahaha.github.io/steinersystems/.
findings.suggested_fix: Describe this as one of the two classical Witt designs, or simply remove the sentence claiming that only two t = 5 systems are known.

findings.description: The docstring’s sentence “Only two explicit examples are known: S(5,6,12) and S(5,8,24)” is false. Other explicit constructions predate Keevash’s existence theorem. This does not affect the correctly stated infinitude theorem or its solved category.
findings.source_evidence: Marwaha’s table, cited by the Epoch problem’s accompanying PDF, says “There is a known Steiner system S(5,6,24)” and “We know of Steiner systems at S(5,6,36) and S(5,6,48)”: https://marwahaha.github.io/steinersystems/. Brouwer lists still more examples and their construction references: https://www.win.tue.nl/~aeb/graphs/S.html.
findings.suggested_fix: Change “Only two explicit examples are known” to “Two classical explicit examples are,” optionally mentioning S(5,6,24) as another known example.

reformulations.difference: The source requests an explicit parameter triple and block list; Lean represents the task as Nonempty LargeSteinerSystemWitness on the zero-based point set Fin n.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Unpacking the structure gives exactly n > k > t > 5, t < 10, n < 200, and a block family satisfying the source’s definition. Relabelling i as i+1 converts Fin n to {1,...,n}. Because the entire bounded search space is finite and validity is decidable, existence permits exhaustive search for an explicit output; the source imposes no running-time bound. The bundle-unpacking equivalence was proved in the scratch file; the full finite-search/relabeling argument was not formalized there.

reformulations.difference: Lean expresses infinitude using a set of labeled structures in Σ k n, S(4,k,n), rather than unbounded orders or infinitely many isomorphism classes.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For fixed n, the condition 4 < k < n allows finitely many k. Each structure is determined by its finite block family on Fin n; its proof fields contribute no additional elements. Thus the projection to n has finite fibers. In the scratch file I proved, for arbitrary t, that the stated infinitude is equivalent to ∀ N, ∃ n > N, ∃ k, t < k ∧ k < n ∧ Nonempty S(t,k,n). This also ensures infinitely many isomorphism classes, since different orders cannot be isomorphic.

reformulations.difference: Lean counts labeled structures in a dependent sum, with k and n varying, rather than directly asserting unbounded orders or counting designs up to isomorphism.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For each n there are finitely many permitted k and finitely many block families on Fin n, and proof irrelevance makes the remaining structure fields immaterial to cardinality. The same generic Lean equivalence proves that this statement is exactly unbounded existence of nontrivial systems with t = 5. Consequently neither relabelings nor proof witnesses can make the infinitude assertion spuriously true.

review.notes: No statement-level misformalizations were found. All findings concern the repeated documentation error about known t = 5 examples. Epoch still records the bounded construction problem as unsolved; Wikipedia and Keevash support the solved infinitude tags. The scratch file /workspace/review/scratch.lean checks the declarations, proves filter-cardinality-one equivalent to unique member-block containment, verifies the bundled bounds, proves the finite-fiber/unbounded-order equivalence without sorry, and tests zero/empty boundary cases. It also computes the Fano plane’s seven blocks and exhaustively excludes S(6,7,8), the smallest numerically permitted triple. Independent checking of the supplied small Witt table found 132 distinct six-element blocks covering all 792 five-element subsets exactly once. All actual problem statements exclude the vacuous t > n cases allowed by the general helper definition. Repository review conventions, all eight non-misformalization examples, the historical index, and five historical fixes were read. Review artifacts were kept under /workspace/review; the reviewed file still matches its committed hash.
